sections.history: Kaleshwaram stands on the bank of the Godavari where the Pranahita joins it, in the Jayashankar Bhupalpally district of northern Telangana. It is counted among the three great Shiva shrines — with Srisailam and Draksharamam — that tradition says marked the bounds of the Trilinga Desham, the 'land of three lingas' from which the name of the Telugu country is often derived. The temple is a modest stone shrine built in the manner of the Kakatiya period, and the Kakatiyas fortified this river crossing between the twelfth and fourteenth centuries. Its sanctity, however, is older than any building: pilgrims have long come to bathe at the confluence, which is revered as the Dakshina Triveni, before seeking the unusual double darshan of Kaleshwara and Mukteswara.
sections.architecture: The temple's heart is its sanctum, where two lingas rise side by side from a single pedestal — Mukteswara, Shiva the liberator, and Kaleshwara, a linga for Yama, the lord of time and death. Such a pairing is rarely seen elsewhere. The Mukteswara linga carries an opening that devotees say never fills however much water is poured in, and local belief holds that it leads by hidden ways to the river. The shrine is built of plain dressed stone in the Kakatiya manner, within an enclosure that also houses subsidiary shrines, and steps lead down from the temple to the bathing ghats at the confluence.
sections.legends: The pairing of the two lingas is the shrine's central teaching: Yama, who ends every life, is worshipped beside Shiva, who grants release from the cycle of birth and death, and pilgrims honour Ganesha first, then Kaleshwara, then Mukteswara. The confluence is called the Dakshina Triveni, for the Godavari and Pranahita are said to be joined by a third, unseen river, the Antarvahini Saraswati. A local story tells of a devout merchant who bathed the linga with pot after pot of milk, and the milk is said to have flowed out into the confluence below.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri draws the largest crowds, and the month of Karthika brings a steady stream of pilgrims for the river bath and lamp worship. Kaleshwaram is also a major centre of the Pushkaralu, the twelve-yearly river festivals of the Godavari, the Pranahita and the Saraswati, when bathers fill the ghats at the confluence. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: A visit begins at the river: pilgrims bathe at the confluence, then climb to the temple to worship Ganesha, Kaleshwara and Mukteswara in turn. The setting is quiet and rural, with wide views over the joined rivers, and the village fills with life on festival days. Kaleshwaram pairs naturally with the Kakatiya temples of Warangal and Palampet on a journey through northern Telangana.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan and a midday closure; Shivaratri, Karthika and the Pushkaralu years bring heavy crowds. Confirm current timings before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected; footwear is removed before entering. Many pilgrims bathe at the confluence first — take care at the river, especially in the monsoon.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted in the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance elsewhere.
visit.gettingThere: Kaleshwaram is in Jayashankar Bhupalpally district, about 60 km from Manthani, 125 km from Karimnagar and 277 km by road from Hyderabad, whose airport is the nearest; buses run from Karimnagar, Manthani and Bhupalpally.
